back: A process that amplifies an initial change, e.g. ice–albedo, water vapour and permafrost carbon feedbacks.
A process that reduces an initial change, e.g. more longwave emission from a warmer Earth, ocean uptake of CO2.
A threshold beyond which change is self-sustaining, often abrupt, and hard to reverse on human timescales.
Melting exposes darker surfaces that absorb more radiation (sea ice albedo about 0.7-0.85 against about 0.06 for open ocean), causing more melting.
If melted completely, Greenland would raise sea level by about 7 m and West Antarctica by about 3 m; loss would take centuries.

front: Slowing of the North Atlantic overturning
back: Meltwater makes surface water less dense, reducing sinking and weakening the circulation that carries warm water north.
Warming, thaw, release of CO2 and methane, more warming, more thaw: a positive feedback.
After a tipping point, a small extra change can cause a disproportionately large and lasting response.
Atmospheric warming melts ice (cold environments); meltwater changes ocean circulation (marine); thawing releases gases to the atmosphere.
